news.title: Putin proposes summit with Trump and Xi to discuss Ukraine deal, WSJ says
news.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a summit next month with US ​President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to negotiate an ‌end to the four-year-old Ukraine conflict that would favour Moscow, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the discussions.

The proposed summit comes amid warming ties ​between Trump and Putin especially after the US President announced a deal to ​buy Russian diesel and signed an order on Friday waiving key sanctions on Moscow.

Citing ⁠a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter, the paper said ​that Putin’s suggestion came in an October 9 telephone call with Trump that ​also yielded the diesel deal between the two countries.

The White House did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment, while the Kremlin could not be immediately reached outside ​regular business hours.

The Russian and Chinese embassies in Washington did not immediately ​reply to requests for comment.

The Kremlin has suggested holding the trilateral dialogue on the sidelines ‌of ⁠the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, the WSJ report said, citing people familiar with the discussions.

That summit is set to take place on November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed to the Journal that discussions were taking place over ​a potential meeting.

“There is ​no clear understanding ⁠yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such ​a meeting taking place,” he told the Wall Street Journal.

A ​senior US ⁠official told the Journal that Trump had not agreed to such a summit, but he could be receptive to the idea.

Trump’s diesel deal with Putin and the ⁠executive ​order waiving sanctions on Moscow have drawn criticism ​from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who has warned it would embolden Putin and prolong the war.

news.title: Indian rupee likely pinned near 95 as RBI defence counters oil headwinds
news.text:
MUMBAI: The Indian rupee is likely to be under pressure from high oil prices at Monday’s open, with the central bank’s dollar sales ​expected to support the currency and keep it near what traders ‌perceive to be the central bank’s soft defence line.

The Indian rupee is expected to open in a 94.92 to 94.98 range, per traders, having settled at 94.96 to the dollar ​on Friday.

The Indian rupee has oscillated around the 95-per-dollar mark in recent ​sessions, briefly strengthening past the level before struggling to sustain it. ⁠Subsequent declines past that level have repeatedly met resistance.

The pattern suggests that ​the Reserve Bank of India may be selling dollars to limit weakness past ​the 95 level, making the level an important near-term support for the currency, a currency trader at a bank said.

The rupee last week posted its best weekly performance in nearly ​four years, buoyed by the RBI’s measures to support the currency and ​repeated dollar sales in the spot market.

The RBI has stepped up its intervention to prop ‌up ⁠the rupee, which remains under pressure from oil prices and capital outflows.

The central bank’s stepped-up defence of the rupee alongside sell/buy swaps is reflected in foreign exchange reserves. The country’s reserves have shed nearly $60 billion since hitting an all-time high ​in the first week of September, ​falling to $726 ⁠billion through October 9.

Oil a pain point

Oil remains a key pressure point for the rupee, with Brent crude briefly climbing ​above $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time ​since May. ⁠

Prices dipped slightly on Monday, with Brent trading around $108 a barrel after US President Donald Trump waived new sanctions on Russia and tariffs on good from Russia, potentially paving ⁠the ​way for increased Russian fuel exports.

There is broad ​consensus among analysts and investors that the RBI’s efforts to support the rupee will go only ​so far unless oil prices retreat.

news.title: Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia
news.text:
Ukrainian attacks set an oil export terminal ablaze in St Petersburg on Sunday, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.

The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

One person was killed and five more were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at both the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, said local Gov. Alexander Beglov. A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center for local tech giant VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.

Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea. 

Meanwhile, a woman died and at least two other people were wounded, including a 6-year-old girl, after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said.

Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged as a result of the attack, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin said.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced on October 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.

Ukraine confirmed Thursday it had resumed attacks on Russian oil after a three-day hiatus.

Zelensky was outraged by Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of his country’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government initially said that it was heeding the ceasefire.

In a post on X Sunday, Zelensky said that in the week since Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times.

He also said that in the past night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.

“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting,” he wrote.

Zelensky also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia’s invasion — not because Ukraine was defending itself.

“It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps,” he said.
news.summary: Ukrainian attacks have set an oil export terminal ablaze in St Petersburg

news.title: Asian stocks slip, Wall St and bonds benefit from oil skid
news.text:
SYDNEY: Asian share markets slipped on Monday as unease ​over AI’s enormous funding needs undermined confidence ahead of a week packed with earnings, while Chinese economic data pipped forecasts in ‌a positive for world growth.

A fall in oil prices offered some support to bonds and Wall Street stock futures, limiting Asia’s losses. Oil fell following US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, though he later said a final decision on the matter had not been made.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on ​Saturday that the president would take up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of such a move. Brent futures ​still fell 1.7% to $107.95 a barrel, while US crude futures lost 0.8% to $100.62 a barrel.

Meanwhile, Iran reported another tanker had ⁠hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz.

Geopolitical tensions combined with safe-haven flows from equities to extend a rally in sovereign bonds, with ​10-year Treasury yields down 4 basis points at 5.0525% , having just recorded their largest weekly fall in over eight months.

All of this helped S&P 500 ​futures edge up 0.7%, while Nasdaq futures rose 1.0%.

Asian markets were hampered by concerns about tech and Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.2%, after losing 5.4% last week. South Korea dropped 0.4%, having shed more than 14% last week, while Taiwan fell 1.4%.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.6%.

“Investors have long worried that AI ​revenues won’t be sufficient to recoup the massive upfront investment, while AI infrastructure may need to be written down as it ages and depreciates ​in the meantime, which lowers book value massively,” said My Bui, an economist at fund manager AMP.

“Rising government bond yields and wider corporate credit spreads are increasing ‌financing costs, ⁠making it harder to borrow, refinance, and keep the AI infrastructure build-out going.”

Chinese blue chips dipped 0.2%, but pared early losses after data showed the economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter to just pip forecasts.

Retail sales were also better with a rise of 1.1%, while industrial output growth came in on forecasts at 5.5%.

A lot riding on earnings

The PHLX ​Semiconductor Index shed 11.4% last week ​in its longest losing streak since ⁠2008.

Investors will be hoping Meta will beat Wall Street forecasts when it reports earnings on Wednesday, along with semiconductor firms Lam Research and Texas Instruments and Elon Musk-led companies SpaceX and Tesla.

Meta is one of five ​AI hyperscalers that combined are expected to increase their capital spending to about $1.2 trillion next year, according ​to Goldman Sachs.

Others reporting ⁠include Netflix, Procter & Gamble, General Motors and GE Aerospace.

Earnings are still expected to rise 30% overall thanks to the huge profits made by tech firms.

European stocks were weighed down by political uncertainty in France with EUROSTOXX 50 futures off 0.3%, while DAX futures lost 0.2% and FTSE futures eased 0.1%.Those same concerns ⁠saw the ​euro ease 0.1% to $1.1232 , nearer to last week’s 16-month low of $1.1113.

The dollar dipped 0.1% ​against the yen to 157.89 and has spent the entire month so far in a tight range as the threat of Japanese intervention has kept speculative sellers at bay.

In commodity ​markets, non-interest-bearing gold got a lift from falling yields and rose 0.4% to $4,181 an ounce .

news.text:

The euro fell 0.1% at $1.1225 as trading began in Asia. ‌The biggest weighting in the dollar index , the common currency’s drop helped steady the greenback, which traded level at 101.83.

French President Emmanuel Macron condemned on Sunday “shocking” scenes of violence on the sidelines of protests over the cost ​of living in a televised address to the nation, a day after France suffered one ​of its worst days of unrest in years.

“The weekend unrest matters for the euro ⁠mainly through French bonds rather than directly,” said Kieran Williams, head of Asia FX at ​InTouch Capital Markets in London.

In emerging market Asia, much of the focus will be on the Indonesian rupiah following a ‌threat from ⁠MSCI to downgrade the country’s stock market to “standalone” status last week, which triggered a 11.6% collapse in equities.

The rupiah hit its weakest level in almost three months on Friday, closing at 18,000 against the dollar.

news.title: As Russia-Ukraine war changes, Zelenskyy could be 'losing a strong partner'
news.text:
From his apartment in Kyiv, Yuriy Sak's attempts to give this interview are interrupted by constant pings on his phone.

They're alerting the former advisor to Ukraine's defence minister another barrage of Russian drones and missiles are on their way.

"It's a new reality we're living in," Mr Sak says, gesturing to an attack visible from outside his window.

It was mid-morning when the ABC spoke to Mr Sak, and he'd already been subjected to several air-raid alarms.

The previous evening, he boarded an overnight train to Kyiv from western Ukraine. At 3am, he says, the carriages ground to a halt and all passengers (including mothers with sleeping babies in their arms) were evacuated to a nearby field, because of an incoming swarm of drones.

With territorial gains on the front lines almost non-existent, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has taken on a different complexion lately.

Moscow's offensive, in its fifth year, has turned its attention to its neighbour's skies.

Since the spring, Russia has intensified aerial attacks on Ukrainian cities, striking civilian targets and critical infrastructure.

Analysts contend the Kremlin is attempting to exploit Ukraine's stretched air defences (it is running particularly short on the US-manufactured Patriot missile interceptors) in an attempt to make life unbearable for people there and pressure the country into accepting its maximalist demands for peace.

Lieutenant General Ben Hodges, a former commander general in Europe for the US Army, told the ABC "strategic bombing" like this "never achieves decisive effect".

"The allies did it against Germany and Japan in World War II. The US did it against North Vietnam and North Korea. The Germans tried it against Great Britain in World War II. It didn't work," he said.

"The populations don't quit. But that's what the Russians are trying to do now."

Starlink speed issue sparks concern

In the past two months, Russia has unleashed improved jet-powered drones on its neighbour.

Some of the latest models can fly at speeds of up to 600 kilometres per hour, making them significantly more difficult to intercept than the first versions that appeared last year.

"Your human eye cannot detect them," Mr Sak said, adding soldiers often end up "randomly shooting in the sky, hoping that one of the bullets will accidentally, randomly hit the drone".

Mr Sak said Ukraine's jet-powered drone interception rate had improved to about 80 per cent in the past month.

But last week, there were unexpected issues.

Overnight into October 14, the speed at which Elon Musk's Starshield internet terminals (the military version of Starlink) could move was capped without warning, according to Ukrainian officials. When they reached speeds of more than 160km/h, connectivity began dropping out.

Ukraine relies on the technology to guide its attack drones and interceptors, and the new cap caused problems.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also accused his country's "partners" of failing to share intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missile attacks during this period. 

Kyiv relies on US intelligence to detect incoming missile attacks. US President Donald Trump has denied his country stopped sending information to Ukraine.

On Sunday, Mr Zelenskyy said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but later "de-blocked".

"We are very thankful for this. Now it works," he told American broadcaster NBC.

Analysts have questioned whether last week's changes that took Ukraine by surprise could have been the White House flexing its muscles.

"I think this was a way of hinting to Ukraine, look guys, if you don't become more agreeable, this is what awaits you … we can pull the plug and you're stuffed," Mr Sak said.

Are the cracks in Ukraine's alliance with Washington that have appeared since Mr Trump re-entered the White House widening?

For his part, Mr Musk denied any involvement in the Starshield changes.

He said any decision to restrict access was not his, because limits on speed and usage are decided by the US military and ultimately the US president.

On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said no-one at the White House ordered the speed to be throttled. 

Zelenskyy says 'we are losing a strong partner'

This year, Kyiv has targeted Russian oil facilities with its drones and missiles, in a bid to hurt the country's economy by torching its largest export, and make life difficult for civilians there.

Ukraine's government describes this as "long-range sanctions" and the tactic has been effective. Last week, Donald Trump demanded they stop doing it, as part of an "energy ceasefire".

Mr Trump announced the ceasefire on October 11, although Ukraine said it knew nothing of the deal.

Mr Trump claims Ukraine's strikes have been pushing up global oil prices, although experts contend the largest rises are actually linked to the US president's war with Iran.

"Ukrainians have the capability now to reach a refinery that is 3,000 kilometres from Ukraine. That's incredible," General Hodges said.

In a significant departure from US foreign policy since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Mr Trump this month announced the US would start buying Russian diesel, something that had been banned by the previous White House administration.

Experts argue the controversial deal is designed to bring petrol prices in the US down ahead of the mid-term elections next month. Polls predict Mr Trump's Republican Party could face a backlash at the ballot box.

Mr Trump said his decision to waive sanctions on Russia was an effort to keep President Vladimir Putin at the negotiating table.

In yet another sign of how relations between Ukraine and the US are deteriorating, Mr Zelenskyy last week gave interviews to Piers Morgan and Britain's Financial Times newspaper, in which he directly criticised Mr Trump.

The usual praise for the US president was gone as the wartime leader labelled his counterpart's recent behaviour a betrayal and raised questions over America's long-term support for Kyiv.

When Morgan asked Mr Zelenskyy, in an interview published on the broadcaster's YouTube channel, whether he felt "betrayed" by Mr Trump, Ukraine's president answered: "Really, yes. Really, between us."

With regard to the US-Ukraine alliance, Mr Zelenskyy said: "It's a pity we are losing a strong partner."

Last week, Mr Trump told US media outlet Newsmax the Ukrainian leader was "more difficult to deal with than Putin".

He also claimed that ongoing Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil infrastructure were "a disgrace", although he did not mention that Moscow had also been trying to strike its neighbour's energy targets.

On Sunday, Mr Zelenskyy told NBC he hoped Mr Trump would change his decisions.

"If the ‌United States will officially take the side of Russia … we will not prevail and we will not be able to stand," he said.
news.summary: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has taken on a different complexion lately, and it has shone a light on Kyiv's strained relations with the White House.
news.author: Kathryn Diss

news.title: Indian shares seen muted; lenders' earnings take centre stage

Indian shares are likely to open little changed on Monday, with investors assessing the results of top private lenders HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, while crude prices above $108 a barrel ​weigh on risk sentiment.

September-quarter ​results will be in focus in this session.

HDFC Bank reported a second-quarter profit that ⁠narrowly missed analyst estimates, as weaker treasury income and higher provisions for bad loans offset ​robust lending growth.

Although US President Donald Trump ‌waived ⁠sanctions and tariffs on Russia, a move that could increase Russian fuel exports and ease supply concerns, persistent Middle East tensions continued to support prices.

Domestic institutional investors outflows stood at a net 36.61 billion rupees, as per NSE’s provisional data.

news.title: State sends wildfire aid to low-income housing while fire victims fight for their homes
news.text:
California officials used federal funding meant to help wildfire victims rebuild, and spent it on low-income housing instead. 

That’s the bombshell revelation in a new report by The California Post. And it confirms the worst suspicions of fire-ravaged communities that have wondered whether state officials ever intended to help them, or simply saw their suffering as an opportunity to exploit.

Beginning with the devastating Camp Fire and Woolsey Fire in 2018, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) allocated almost a billion dollars to California.

The money was meant to help rebuild homes, provide affordable rental housing, and repair infrastructure.

But the state allocated $368.7 million to developers to build dense, low-income housing projects, without any guarantee fire victims would benefit.

To this day, there are families who have not returned home. Some lived in trailers on their lots until local officials ordered them removed, and others don’t have the money to rebuild.

The push for low-income housing accomplishes three ideological goals. One, it redistributes property from those who had it to those who do not. 

Two, it satisfies a “green” agenda that sees single-family homes as a sign of wasteful sprawl. 

And three, it allows politicians to claim they are doing something about the state’s housing crisis.

But none of that is the purpose of the funding, which taxpayers provided to help rebuild communities that had been destroyed through no fault of their own.

It is no longer a conspiracy theory to say that some policymakers would rather see residents of destroyed communities replaced by dense developments than to see them safely restored to their homes. 

We hear a lot from California Governor Gavin Newsom about how he is not to blame for the fact that President Donald Trump and the Republican Congress have yet to provide additional funding for rebuilding after the devastating LA wildfires in 2025. 

But perhaps Washington has been reluctant for good reason: Americans cannot trust that California will spend the money properly.

We have noted before that politics should never get in the way of emergency relief. This it about getting politics out of fire aid. California politicians are the ones who have misallocated fire relief funds.

The saddest part of this story is that the need is still urgent. Thousands of fire victims still need help. And the federal government should provide it. But strict oversight should come along with it.
news.summary: California officials used federal funding meant to help wildfire victims rebuild, and spent it on low-income housing instead.

news.title: As obstacles to peace go, Zelenskyy ranks below Trump
news.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy is again in a throwdown with the president of the United States, this time over his refusal to obey a White House edict to stop bombing Russian oil refineries. So has the former comedian who rules Kyiv become the main barrier to peace, as both the Kremlin and now Donald Trump say?This is not, after all, the only trouble Ukraine’s leader is having. He’s also in a diplomatic fight with South Korea and at loggerheads with his own country’s anti-corruption agencies, which are investigating some of his closest associates. Indeed, if it were not for the war, Zelenskyy likely would be long gone, voted out in a routine election.And yet the correct response to Trump telling Ukrainians they need to pick a new leader willing to strike a deal with the Kremlin is: Are you kidding? Indeed, in the hierarchy of politicians responsible for the continuation of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Zelenskyy ranks only third, after Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump himself.
news.summary: In the hierarchy of politicians responsible for the continuation of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Zelenskyy ranks only third, after Putin and Trump.

news.title: Democrats remain clear favourites to gain control of Congress at midterms
news.text:
With just over two weeks until the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats have a three in four chance to gain control of the Senate, and remain overwhelming favourites to gain control of the House of Representatives in Nate Silver’s forecast model.

Democrats lead Republicans by 9.6 points on the generic ballot, and Donald Trump’s net approval is -22.3.

If disruption caused by the Iran war continues until the midterm elections, with increased petrol prices and inflation, Republicans are likely to lose control of both the House and the Senate, perhaps with huge losses.

With the oil price surging recently, petrol prices are likely to increase again before the midterms.

Trump’s ratings

In Silver’s aggregate of US national polls, Trump’s net approval is -22.3. Currently, 59.8% disapprove of his performance and 37.6% approve. There haven’t been many polls taken since Trump’s October 9 announcement of a diesel import deal with Russia.

Trump’s net approval was -22.5 in my October 7 article, but fell to a record low of -23.9 on October 9 before a slight recovery. His net approval had improved to -18.7 on September 4 before falling back.

Trump’s net approval is below what any past president since Harry Truman had at this point in their term, with Joe Biden the closest at -11.7.

On four issues tracked by Silver, Trump’s net approval is -11.6 on immigration, -30.6 on trade, -32.9 on the economy and -48.9 on inflation. Since my October 7 article, Trump’s net approval on trade has dropped two points, but has improved one point on immigration.

Silver also has an aggregate of US support for the Iran war. Currently, 56.2% are opposed to the Iran war while 35.2% support it, for a net support of -21.0, up from a record low of -27.9 in my October 7 article. 

Midterm elections on November 3

All 435 federal House of Representatives seats and 35 of the 100 senators will be up for election at November 3 midterm elections.

In 2024 elections, Republicans won the House by 220–215 over Democrats and the Senate by 53–47. Owing to Vice President JD Vance’s potential tie-breaking vote, Democrats need at least a four-seat gain to win Senate control.

As I previously wrote, owing to Republican gerrymandering, Democrats need at least a four-point margin in the generic ballot to have a good chance to win the House majority. The Senate is more skewed to Republicans as every state has two senators. Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win the Senate on a uniform swing.

In Silver’s midterm election forecast model, the generic ballot gives Democrats a 51.3–41.7 lead over Republicans, a 9.6-point margin (up from 9.2 points last Wednesday, but the same 9.6 points as in my October 7 article). Democrats’ lead had dropped to 7.4 points on September 4.

Polls that screen for likely voters usually give Democrats larger leads than polls that ask registered voters. Democrats are more likely to vote at lower turnout elections like the midterms than Republicans, when Trump is not on the ballot.

Silver’s model gives Democrats a 75% chance to win the Senate and a 94% chance to win the House, respectively 74% and 93% on October 7. Democratic chances to win the Senate had fallen to a low of 50% on September 7, and their chances of winning the House had dropped to 81% on September 3.

While uniform swing indicates that Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win control of the Senate, Silver’s model has Democrats as the favourites to win with a 5–6 point margin in the generic ballot. In the House, Democrats are favourites if they win by 2–3 points.

 Read more:
 The American mood is turning dark, and Republicans are likely to pay the price at the midterms

Democrats lead Republicans by one to four points in polls of Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Alaska and Ohio. Trump won all these states by double-digit margins in 2024. In Nebraska, a Republican is only 0.1 points ahead of an independent. But Democrats are only leading by 2.8 points in Maine, which Kamala Harris won by 6.9 points.

Silver said on Saturday that Democrats lead in polls of 54 Senate races (including seats not up for election). If polls are basically right nationally, Democrats have an 88% chance to win the Senate, with an average of 52.4 senators.

If polls are systematically overstating Democrats by 3–4 points nationally, Democrats’ chance of winning the Senate drops to 38%, with an average of 49.7 senators. But if polls are understating Democrats by 3–4 points nationally, their chance to win the Senate rises to 99% with an average of 54.6 senators.

Economic data

Americans are currently paying an average of US$4.30 a gallon for regular petrol (gasoline in the US), down from US$4.36 a gallon in my October 7 article and US$4.48 on September 25. Owing to profits and taxes, the retail price of petrol will be higher than the commodity price.

The commodity price of petrol had surged from a low of US$2.99 a gallon on August 27 to US$3.59 on September 23, but has fallen back to its current US$3.19 a gallon.

However, the international benchmark Brent oil has surged from US$96.16 a barrel on September 29 to US$109.86 last Friday, the highest it has been since May. There appears to be a lag between changes in oil prices and petrol prices, so petrol prices are likely to increase again before the midterms.

In Silver’s models, Trump and Republicans were at a high in early September, shortly after the August 27 low point in petrol prices.

The September inflation report was released last Wednesday. Owing to high petrol prices, inflation increased 0.6% in September, up from 0.4% in August. Core inflation was up 0.3%, the same as in August. Annual inflation was 3.7%, the highest it has been before the midterms since 1990, except during COVID. Core annual inflation was 2.6%.

Real (inflation-adjusted) wages fell 0.5% in both hourly and weekly terms in September owing to high inflation and low wage growth. Annual real wages were down 0.7% in hourly terms and down 0.1% in weekly terms.

After combined losses of 1.9% in the last three trading sessions, the benchmark US S&P stock market index was down 2.0% last Friday from its October 6 peak. But it was still up 10.3% from its peak in the week before the Iran war began in late February and up 16.2% from its worst point in the Iran war in late March.

news.title: ‘60 Minutes’ Legend Goes In On Trump After Bust-Up With Boss Is Leaked
news.text:
60 Minutes legend Lesley Stahl delivered a scathing report on President Donald Trump’s federal election-meddling efforts just a week after an alleged editorial dust-up with her MAGA-curious boss, Bari Weiss.

Stahl, 84, dove deep into how the Trump administration has attempted to undermine the reliability of elections, speaking with state and local officials about their unprecedented actions regarding election security on Sunday night’s episode.

The 35-year-veteran correspondent first spoke with Fulton County Commissioner Dana Barrett about the administration’s January FBI raid on a local Georgia election facility.

“In my wildest dreams, I never imagined that we would be raided by the FBI,” Barrett, a Democrat, told Stahl on 60 Minutes.

In January, FBI officials stormed the Fulton County election office and seized hundreds of boxes containing ballots and voter rolls from the 2020 presidential election.

Barrett described how dozens of federal agents, wearing vests and carrying guns, arrived at the warehouse with a criminal search warrant. She told Stahl she had no choice but to let them seize the ballots they were looking for, and that to this day, she still has no idea where they went.

“I think it was all part of this concerted effort that’s happening nationwide to undermine faith in elections,” she said.

Stahl also spoke with Utah Republican Lieutenant Governor Deidre Henderson, who agreed that the level of federal interference in elections was unheard of.

“In the past two elections that I oversaw as lieutenant governor, the threats were all external. Non-state actors, cybersecurity threats, and other things,” she said. “But now we also have threats coming from within our own government.”

Henderson described how Trump’s Justice Department demanded their “statewide voter registration list,” which includes voters’ sensitive personal information.

“They wanted things that we typically are required by law to keep private: Social Security numbers, full dates of birth, driver’s license numbers,” she said, noting that DOJ officials didn’t explain why they needed the confidential data.

Henderson dismissed the government’s claim that noncitizen voting was a major problem, saying she found only 52 cases among the over 2 million votes cast in Utah. Stahl said that the figure calculated out to two-thousandths of one percent.

The Utah Republican said the DOJ notified her last month that she was officially “under investigation,” but that she wouldn’t back down even despite the federal pressure.

“I’m just doing my job,” she told Stahl. “I have to tell myself it doesn’t matter what the consequences are, if—as long as I feel like I’m doing what’s right.”

Henderson continued, “I think this is an important thing for me to do—holding these guardrails, holding the line. Someone has to.”

Stahl then turned her attention to Trump.

“In America, elections are local. They’re run by towns and counties and states. It’s all in Article 1 of the Constitution. Congress makes laws regulating elections,” she explained. “But the president doesn’t have a role in running them. That hasn’t stopped Mr. Trump from signing two executive orders trying to create new federal voting rules.”

She also highlighted just how frequently Trump, 80, has belabored his claims of election fraud in the 2020 election.

“In the 21 months of President Trump’s second term, he has said, in so many words, the vote can’t be trusted more than 150 times,” Stahl said. 

Speaking with the DOJ’s assistant attorney general for civil rights, Harmeet Dhillon, Stahl pressed the Trump appointee on whether the president would go so far as to station federal ICE agents to polling locations.

“There is no plan to do that,” Dhillon, 57, answered, adding that the idea that Trump would challenge the midterm results was just “paranoia.”

“I don’t know what is going to happen, but I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states,” she told Stahl.

Stahl’s in-depth report on Trump comes just a week after a claim that she had a heated debate with CBS News editor-in-chief Weiss over a 60 Minutes segment on violent Israeli settlers.

Insiders revealed to Status that Weiss, a fervent supporter of Israel and critic of media coverage in Gaza, inserted herself repeatedly into the editorial process behind the report and became “very, very hands-on.”

Weiss and her deputy, managing editor Charles Forelle, were even thinking of shelving the report for a later date, but Stahl wasn’t having it.

Stahl and Weiss then engaged in an “aggressive back-and-forth,” which resulted in the story coming to air last Sunday.

The 60 Minutes veteran, however, privately discussed quitting, according to Status.

“This is a ludicrous, twisted narrative. All ‘60 Minutes’ pieces go through a famously rigorous editorial process—which includes edits from editors. This piece received far fewer edits than most,” a CBS spokesperson said of the report at the time.

news.title: France on fire: City halls set ablaze, shops looted as protests turn violent - videos
news.text: France witnessed widespread destruction, looting and clashes with police as nationwide protests over the rising cost of living and poor conditions in schools escalated into violence, leaving businesses damaged and public buildings in flames. President Emmanuel Macron has vowed legal action against rioters while announcing measures to address public grievances.The scale of the unrest was visible in Paris on Sunday, where shattered shopfronts, broken glass and dislodged cobblestones littered the area around Place de la République. It is an extremely serious and unspeakable act,” Barate said.In Marseille, protesters briefly entered the City Hall lobby, while a group damaged a police station. news.title: ‘Moderate’ Elissa Slotkin pretends she’s a stickler for ‘defending democracy’ — but this is how the Bolshevik left play the game
news.text:
Elissa Slotkin was elected to the Senate in 2024 as a supposed “moderate.”

But of course we know that, apart from Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman, that species of Democratic politician doesn’t exist in Congress anymore.

Sure enough, it didn’t take long for Slotkin, a former CIA analyst who served under John Brennan, to show her true colors.

The Michigan senator told students at the University of Chicago last week how she plans to use the power that will come to Democrats if they win Senate control in the midterms next month.

She wants to unleash a barrage of political investigations on Trump officials in order to frighten young people away from taking jobs in the administration.

“The people around Donald Trump . . . have no immunity the way the president does . . . So you go after the people who do his bidding,” she told the audience during a live podcast recording Tuesday.

‘Signature cases’

“I want to look at these signature cases and not just focus on the president, but on the people who enabled him,” she continued.

“I want young people coming out of school to say, ‘Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like that sounds fun. I might get an opportunity.’

“I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that.’

“I want that deterrence message.”

Slotkin pretends she is a stickler for “defending democracy.” But this is how the Bolshevik left who control today’s Democratic Party play the game, even as they cloak themselves in conservative disguises, as intelligence professionals, soldiers, astronauts or doctors.

Slotkin, who fancies herself as a future president, used that same term “signature cases” in a chilling speech to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in September when she named Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, DC US Attorney Jeanine Pirro and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem as the Trump officials she would target for political prosecutions that would see them jailed for 20 years.

She likened her planned revenge campaign against Trump officials to Poland’s “Iron Broom” cleanup, in which Democrats would create “a list of signature cases that go after some of the most obvious and harmful abuses of taxpayer dollars.”

“We need to hold accountable the people and institutions who stole billions of our taxpayer dollars and weaponized the government against its people,” she said.

“In Poland, they called this plan the Iron Broom — cleaning the place up.”

Slotkin’s threats are especially disturbing when you consider the body count of administration officials and Trump allies from the president’s first term who were attacked by Joe Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.

It’s one aspect of the psychological warfare she learned in her former intelligence career.

Last year, Slotkin and five other “national security” Democrats launched a sly propaganda video implying that Trump was giving “illegal orders” to the military.

They pretended the video was a public service to inform military members that they were not obliged to follow the orders of the commander in chief.

Senate in play

Trump and War Secretary Pete Hegseth accused them of sedition, and Slotkin later admitted in an interview that Trump had never issued any illegal orders and therefore their video was a psyop. But they got away with sowing doubt among the troops.

In May, Slotkin traveled to Canada to meet the nation’s prime minister, Mark Carney, and stir up trouble at a summit organized by the left-wing Center for American Progress where liberal politicians from around the globe discussed “how to battle right-wing politicians on affordability.” In other words, how to defeat Trump.

In another case of lefties sticking together, Carney since has been accused of interfering with our midterm elections by kiboshing US-Canada trade negotiations in August and placing additional economic pressure on the border Senate battleground states of Maine and Michigan — Slotkin’s home base.

Slotkin and her fellow CIA wolf-in-sheep’s clothing, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, are especially dangerous because they present as non-threatening soccer mom types when they really are hardcore ideologues who have learned the dark art of manipulating democracies around the world to suit their purposes.

Therefore, Slotkin speaks in the language of calm, reasonable moderation while governing like a revolutionary.

The Senate is stuck with her until 2030, but the last thing conservatives should do is sign their own death warrants by bolstering her numbers, sitting on their hands on Nov. 3 or even voting for the other side out of resentment over Trump not delivering everything he promised in two years.

After all, despite the gloomy polls and wall-to-wall negative media coverage, the Senate is salvageable for Republicans, even if the House follows historical precedent and falls to the Democrats.

As Harry Enten, CNN’s chief data analyst, pointed out last week, polls are within an average margin of error of 3.7 percentage points, so the Senate at this point is too close to call.

“If Republican candidates outperform the [poll] averages by 3.75 points, Republicans would get 52 seats, Democrats would get 48,” he said.

Republicans also have buffers in the Senate, even if they lose three seats.

France a warning

JD Vance, as vice president, is the president of the Senate and can cast the deciding vote in any 50-50 deadlock.

There’s another potential buffer in the form of the aforementioned Sen. Fetterman. As Julian Epstein, former chief counsel for the House Judiciary Democrats, wrote recently in these pages, Fetterman has teased the possibility of flipping parties if he ends up holding the balance of power.

“I don’t have a reason” to jump ship to the Republicans, Fetterman told CBS three weeks ago. But if he becomes the Senate’s 51st Democrat and the deciding vote, he suggested he might rethink his position.

“If I’m 51,” he said, “then I don’t know. Let’s revisit after the midterms.”

Fetterman understands, as all decent Democrat voters do, that the malign Bolshevik force that has overtaken their party must be defeated before it can be trusted with power again.

Slotkin and her fellow Jewish Democrats who embrace the new Islamo-Marxist green-red alliance are like the appeasers Winston Churchill accused in World War II of feeding the crocodile in the hope he eats them last.

The violent chaos on the streets of France shows us our own future if the ascendant revolutionary left gains a foothold.

news.title: Zelensky offered Russia strike deal: US senator
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 19 (IANS) Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has offered to stop attacks on Russian energy facilities in exchange for expanded American satellite targeting capabilities that would allow Ukrainian forces to strike missile and drone launch sites deep inside Russia, a senior Republican senator disclosed. Senator Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said the proposal was presented to Zelensky during a recent visit to Ukraine and received an enthusiastic response from the Ukrainian leader. The initiative was developed by Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and subsequently discussed with officials in Washington, Cramer told CBS's Face the Nation. The proposed arrangement would allow Ukraine to redirect its attacks from Russian energy infrastructure towards military installations used to launch strikes against Ukrainian territory. "So, that – you're right, that was a proposal we brought to President Zelensky. Senator Wicker, Roger Wicker, the chairman of the Armed Services Committee, came up with that idea," Cramer said. "President Zelensky was enthusiastic about it. He said, I can do that tomorrow." According to Cramer, Zelensky indicated that Ukraine would immediately halt attacks on Russian energy facilities if Washington provided expanded access to Starshield, the military satellite communications and targeting system associated with SpaceX. The proposed capabilities would enable Ukrainian forces to identify and attack Russian launch facilities beyond their current operational reach. "I would absolutely stop attacking Russia's energy facilities if I could have access to targeting capabilities, which is what Starshield would provide them, to go deep into Russia and attack their attackers," Cramer said, recounting Zelensky's response. The senator described the military objective as targeting the source of Russian attacks rather than intercepting incoming weapons. "And, you know, kill the archer, not the arrows," he said. Cramer also disclosed that Zelensky had sought American permission to jointly manufacture Patriot missile interceptors, which Ukraine needs to defend against increasingly sophisticated Russian missiles and drones. "Of course, the third thing he asked for was the capacity to get license to jointly produce, co-produce Patriot missile interceptors," Cramer said. He said the additional interceptors would strengthen Ukraine's defences against faster, jet-powered drones and missiles. Cramer expressed support for all three Ukrainian requests, including stronger enforcement of American sanctions against Russia. "So, his requests were three, they were simple, and I agree with all three of them," he said. The senator confirmed that the proposal had been discussed with officials at the White House, the Pentagon and the State Department before the delegation met Zelensky. He also said the administration remained involved in negotiations, although he had not personally discussed the latest proposal with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Cramer acknowledged that no agreement had yet been reached on expanding Starshield access. He called for restoring Ukraine's existing satellite capabilities and providing targeting assistance for strikes farther inside Russian territory. "Certainly Congress itself could and should investigate," he said, referring to the recent interruption of satellite services affecting Ukrainian operations. The disclosure comes as Washington faces disagreements over military assistance to Ukraine and President Donald Trump's decision to suspend enforcement of new sanctions targeting Russia and countries trading with Moscow.

news.title: Trump Insider Spills on ‘Terrifying’ Ice Maiden Replacement Rumor
news.text:
A former Trump aide is sounding the alarm about who could replace the president’s White House chief of staff.

Sarah Matthews was a deputy press secretary during Donald Trump’s first term. On Sunday, she told MeidasTouch that the president seems to be turning on his Chief of Staff, Susie Wiles.

“It seems like Trump is unhappy with the way things are right now and the headlines and the way his administration is going, so he is seeming to blame Susie Wiles.” Matthews, 31, told host Jack Cocchiarella. 

“She’s kind of on the outs, and he’s been doing his favorite thing, which is calling around, seeing what people think of different names that he floats,” she said. 

“He said that he’s sticking with Susie, but we know that he’s making these calls. And one of those names is Stephen Miller.” 

Politico Playbook reported Thursday that Trump has been sounding out confidants about Wiles, 69, and asking who could replace her. Besides Miller, the president reportedly floated special envoy Steve Witkoff, housing chief Bill Pulte, former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, and Yankees president Randy Levine as possible successors. The report set off a catfight as Wiles and her allies scrambled to shore up her position.

Matthews didn’t mince her words about what a Miller promotion would mean for America.

“That is a terrifying prospect, because I think that Susie Wiles, while she is complicit in the horrors of this administration, I don’t think she’s crazy,” Matthews said. “Stephen Miller is bats--t crazy.” 

“In the last two years of Trump’s administration, when he’s going to be spiraling because he’s a lame duck president, I think he’s going to pardon everyone at the end. So he thinks he can get away with murder,” she added. “The idea of someone like a Stephen Miller in charge is a very scary thing.”

But Trump insists he isn’t looking for a replacement. 

“Susie Wiles is my loyal and longest-serving Chief of Staff — there is a reason for that,” he said in a statement to Politico on Thursday.

“She has been with me since the beginning, is my trusted advisor, and has my COMPLETE confidence.”

Cocchiarella asked Matthews how much time she had spent with Miller during her tenure. 

Matthews said Miller sometimes sat in on briefing prep, “something that we spent hours doing that -clearly Katie Zacharia did not.”

Trump fired Zacharia, 41, on Friday, after only five days on the job. Her departure came after a shaky 14-minute debut briefing and days of questions about her credentials, after she admitted she never passed the bar exam.

“When we were prepping Kayleigh for briefings, Stephen would sometimes come into her office and help consult if we felt like we needed his guidance on something or advice,” Matthews said. 

“Him and I would chit-chat here and there, but we weren’t particularly close.”

Matthews was a deputy to Kayleigh McEnany, Trump’s press secretary at the time, and helped drill her before her televised briefings.

Then the host asked whether Miller is “as insecure as it seems he is publicly.”

“I have to imagine that a guy who spray paints hair on his head before going on a TV interview is about as insecure as you can get,” Matthews said. She appeared to be referring to a 2018 Vanity Fair report that said Miller showed up on CBS’ Face the Nation with spray-painted hair on top of his usually bald head. 

Miller, a loyal Trump ally who has worked for him for a decade, is the driving force behind the administration’s mass deportation push. 

He stepped out of public view after federal agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during an immigration operation in Minneapolis in January. He kept running the crackdown from inside the West Wing, the Times reported in April. Insiders have described his daily calls with immigration officials as screaming sessions. 

Matthews resigned after the Jan. 6 riot and has been a vocal critic of the Trump administration ever since. 

In August, she described Natalie Harp as one of Trump’s “gatekeepers of information.”

According to Playbook, Harp handed Trump a printout of Thursday’s report, and he reportedly erupted. Miller, Pulte, and EPA chief Lee Zeldin are already circling like vultures, making moves for her job, the Washington Post reports. 

Trump biographer Michael Wolff has his own prediction. “After the midterms, she will be toast,” he said on the Daily Beast’s Inside Trump’s Head podcast. “Susie toast.”

“I don’t think getting inside the mind of Stephen Miller is a place I want to be,” Matthews said.

The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast’s request for comment.

MANDEL NGAN / AFP via Getty ImagesA former Trump aide is sounding the alarm about who could replace the president’s White House chief of staff.

Sarah Matthews was a deputy press secretary during Donald Trump’s first term. On Sunday, she told MeidasTouch that the president seems to be turning on his Chief of Staff, Susie Wiles.

“It seems like Trump is unhappy with the way things are right now and the headlines and the way his administration is going, so he is seeming to blame Susie Wiles.” Matthews, 31, told host Jack Cocchiarella.

news.title: Trump backs ally Netanyahu ahead of Israel's tight election
news.text: JERUSALEM — US President Donald Trump endorsed on Sunday his ally Benjamin Netanyahu before Israel's close-fought parliamentary election on October 27, providing a boost to the veteran prime minister's bid to win a new mandate.Netanyahu touted his close relationship with the US president in a video released by his Likud party, saying that together they had 'crushed Iran' and adding that re-election would allow him to work with Trump to 'elminate the Iranian threat over the next two years, or even sooner'.The endorsement comes less than two weeks before Israel's first vote since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, which opposition politicians have accused Netanyahu of bearing personal responsibility for after allegedly ignoring warnings.Trump and Netanyahu, who polls show is in a tight election race, have worked closely together on Israel's multi-front wars after the Hamas-led attack, including bombarding Iran, and the endorsement could be a boon to his re-election campaign.'Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,' Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, using a common nickname for the Israeli leader.'This is the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much. Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.'The election is seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, who quickly thanked the US leader for his support on Sunday.'Thank you, President Trump, for your tremendous support and for our work together. Together we will complete the mission!' he wrote on X.'I ask you to listen carefully to what President Trump said this evening,' Netanyahu told voters. 'He said that together we have accomplished extraordinary things... But there is still a mission to complete.'Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned Netanyahu was 'driving America into another war'.'Last time you wanted to 'finish the job', Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too,' Araghchi wrote on X.Trump joined Netanyahu in a US-Israeli attack on Iran in late February but agreed to a ceasefire in April in the face of widespread US public opposition to the war, which had sent oil prices spiralling.Speaking at an event in August, Netanyahu said Trump 'is our greatest friend, one of the greatest friends we have had in the White House'.But relations between the two have at times been strained on Iran, with Netanyahu saying no diplomatic agreement was possible with Iran's leadership, while Trump sought a negotiated end to the months-long conflict.Voter warning The endorsement comes after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned against a brewing 'crisis' in the occupied West Bank after an American photojournalist for The Washington Post was injured in a brutal attack by Israeli settlers.'We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing,' Rubio told reporters Saturday. Netanyahu's office said it was investigating the circumstances around the attack.With Israel and Netanyahu looking increasingly isolated on the world stage, Trump's support is vital.Netanyahu, who turns 77 on October 21, is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, having served on and off for more than 19 years.The wily political operator returned to power in December 2022, bringing in once-shunned ultra-nationalists and quickly tried to rein in the judiciary, which is examining corruption charges that could land him in jail.His main election rival is opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the centre-right Yashar party and a former military chief who regularly accuses Netanyahu of bearing personal responsibility for the October 7 attack.About seven million Israelis will be eligible to vote in the legislative election.Current polls show that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor that led by Eisenkot is in a position to win the 61 seats needed to control the 120-seat parliament and form a governing coalition.Eisenkot said that only Israelis could choose who they want to run the country.Speaking at a conference in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot said he 'admires' Trump 'but Israel is a democratic country, only Israelis can choose their leaders'.But Trump warned against Israel electing 'anyone other than Bibi', writing that if voters chose one of his rivals, 'America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so'.

news.title: Unhinged Trump Makes Shock Confession Over Sweetheart Deal With Putin
news.text:
President Donald Trump has confessed that his sweetheart deal with Vladimir Putin is part of a plan to keep the Russian leader happy.

Trump, 80, waived sanctions and tariffs on Russia as part of an executive order he signed on Friday, just two days before they were due to take effect. Trump’s friend, MAGA Senator Lindsey Graham, lobbied for the bill before he died in July. When Congress passed it last month, it was named after the late Russia hawk.

The shock order followed Trump allowing Russia to export diesel to the U.S. earlier this month in a move to drop fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, as his war with Iran continues to impact energy prices. Gas prices are sitting at a national average of just under $4.30 per gallon with the midterm elections weeks away.

In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump called his decision on lifting sanctions on Russia “a very simple one.”

“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he wrote of the war, which began in 2014, before escalating with Russia’s full-scale military invasion into Ukraine in February 2022.

He added, “Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations! Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!”

Trump also claimed in his post that Russia is not helping Iran in their war with the U.S. “compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way.”

He also blamed Ukrainian President Trump Volodymyr Zelensky for using diesel refineries in Russia “as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States.”

He added, “Farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this, but Russia is, nevertheless, sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World.”

Trump also claimed his Ukrainian counterpart “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”

The senior president’s post ended “I WANT THIS WAR END!,” presumably forgetting the word “to.”

During an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Zelensky said America formally siding with Putin would be a “historic mistake.”

He added that America pulling support will have dire consequences for his country. 

“It’s all about losses... it’s about our people,” Zelensky said. “If United States will support Putin, it’s unbelievable... it’s historic mistake and big tragedy.”

He said Ukraine needs to be pragmatic, adding, “If the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail.”

Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNN’s State of the Union that the Trump administration is putting pressure on Russia, not Ukraine, with the energy deal.

“Russia does not have diesel to export,” Wright told host Dana Bash. “The only way they can get additional diesel to export is if they turn down the conflict with Ukraine. They have to either get an energy ceasefire, they have to either end the war or they have to reduce their war efforts so they have additional diesel to export. This is not a going soft on Russia, this is an incentive to end the war.”

Wright also claimed Trump is looking for a “different way” to find peace.

“This is quite innovative, actually. What does the world need most of all for energy right now? Diesel. What is Russia not able to supply right now? Diesel. This is a motivation for Russia to figure out how they can actually export some diesel.”

Three Republican senators called for Trump to “immediately reverse” his diesel importation last week, which had been in place since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

After Trump signed his executive order, Texas Republican John Cornyn posted on X, “Lindsey would be appalled.” He added on Saturday on X: “Helping Putin in Ukraine is reckless. He would not stop with Ukraine and our NATO allies would be next.”

Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who Trump has backed in South Carolina, took a calmer response than Cornyn.

“Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” Graham said at a midterm campaign event in South Carolina on Sunday. “Because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia.”

The White House referred the Daily Beast to Trump’s Truth Social post when asked for comment.

news.title: Trump Admin Pauses Russia Sanctions For 60 Days, Rubio Says India In Focus
news.text:
The Donald Trump administration will take 60 days to assess the potential global economic impact of imposing sweeping new sanctions on Russia and its trading partners, including India, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday.
Explaining Washington's decision to waive sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Act this week, Rubio pointed to mounting pressure on global energy prices amid the war in Ukraine, the conflict involving Iran and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Rubio made the remarks while speaking to reporters ahead of his visit to Uzbekistan and India, highlighting the need to weigh the economic consequences of fresh restrictions against the broader geopolitical situation.
Why Trump Is Reviewing Russia Sanctions
Rubio said the legislation included provisions for waivers to give the administration time to assess the implications of its measures, particularly amid disruptions to global energy supplies.
He noted that the pressure on energy markets was not limited to the conflict involving Iran or disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. Attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia and strikes on energy infrastructure amid the Russia-Ukraine war were also affecting global prices, he said.
The US secretary of state said Washington needed to consider these factors together before determining the appropriate combination of measures against Russia and countries buying its energy.
How The Lindsey Graham Act Could Affect India
Rubio also highlighted the potential implications of the legislation for India, which continues to purchase Russian energy despite diversifying its sources of supply.
The law authorises the US president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest purchasers of Russian energy. Rubio acknowledged that India remained an important US partner and said shifting away from Russian supplies could not happen overnight.
" So we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is," Rubio said, explaining why the administration needed time to evaluate the consequences of the measures.
Trump Invokes Waiver To Hold Off Tariffs
Just a month after signing the Lindsey Graham Act into law, Trump invoked its waiver provision on Friday to defer tariffs of up to 100% that could otherwise have been imposed on India and four other countries for purchasing Russian oil and gas.
The order also waived several sanctions targeting Russia and its economic partners on national interest grounds, with the exemptions remaining in place until further notice.
Beyond tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy, the legislation gives the president the authority to raise tariffs on Russian exports to the US to as much as 500%. It also permits tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest countries helping Russia circumvent oil sanctions.
The law further provides for additional sanctions targeting Russian financial institutions and their international partners, with the broader objective of pressuring Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
US Energy Prices Add To Pressure On Trump
The decision to grant the waivers also comes as the Trump administration seeks to bring down domestic energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections scheduled for November 3.
Last week, the administration announced a controversial diesel supply arrangement with Russia that could see Moscow provide 5 million tonnes of diesel to the US and the global market in the coming months.
Trump explicitly linked the arrangement to his efforts to lower energy costs for American consumers, underscoring the role of fuel prices in the administration's economic calculations.
The 60-day review will give Washington time to weigh its efforts to pressure Russia over the Ukraine war against the potential consequences of further restrictions for global energy markets and partners such as India.

news.title: US intelligence blackout hurt Ukraine: Zelensky
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 19 (IANS) Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that the United States temporarily suspended crucial intelligence sharing with Ukraine for three days, leaving its forces without American warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks during that period. In an interview with NBC's Meet the Press, Zelensky also said restrictions on satellite communications used by Ukrainian forces had not been fully lifted, raising fresh questions about Washington's military and intelligence support for Kyiv. The Ukrainian leader said the intelligence interruption affected information that only the United States could provide, particularly advance warnings of ballistic missile strikes. "We didn’t see attacks of Russia using ballistic missiles," Zelensky said. He said Ukraine continued receiving intelligence from European governments and other international partners, but their capabilities could not fully replace American systems. "We have dozens of countries who help. But only United States has this unique intelligence to say, to tell us, to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles," he said. "And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days." Zelensky said the intelligence-sharing arrangement had since been restored. "It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works," he said. The disclosure came amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over President Donald Trump's handling of the war with Russia. Zelensky also raised concerns about restrictions affecting Starlink, the satellite internet network operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and its military-related services. Asked whether the interruption had been deliberate, Zelensky said Ukrainian military officials believed the restrictions originated with the American government. "Of course the message came from government. I don’t know from whom, what cabinet, and etc," he said. He added that Ukrainian officials believed SpaceX had technically implemented the restrictions following instructions from Washington. Zelensky acknowledged that he did not know which American official might have authorised the move. Asked whether satellite services had been fully restored, he replied: "No, not of course. We have limitation." The Ukrainian President's account was challenged by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared separately on the same programme. Bessent said Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had denied that anyone in the administration ordered restrictions on Starlink. "President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that," Bessent said. He called Zelensky's allegation reckless and said he had no information about the reported intelligence interruption. "Again, I don’t know anything about that, but we’ve been very clear," Bessent said. The conflicting accounts left unresolved who was responsible for the communications disruption and why American intelligence sharing had been temporarily interrupted. Zelensky said Ukraine remained dependent on American military assistance despite its growing network of European partners. "If it’s without United States’ support, it’s very difficult," he said. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Since then, American intelligence, weapons and satellite communications have played an important role in Ukraine's defence against Russian military operations, including missile and drone attacks.

news.title: Why Trump’s Potty Mouth Is Raising Eyebrows: Fired ABC Star
news.text:
Donald Trump’s increasingly profane language is a sign of his cognitive decline, one veteran journalist alleges.

Terry Moran, a longtime ABC journalist who was dismissed by the network last year after calling out the “hatred” within top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, told The Daily Beast Podcast host Joanna Coles that the 80-year-old president has increasingly relied on profanity as he has gotten older.

“The president’s potty mouth is...his own liberation,” Moran said.

“We’ve all seen him evolve over time. He’s not as sharp as he used to be on the stump...He had an almost carnivorous sense of where the vulnerabilities and the excitement in the crowd were, and he’d riff, riff them up. And now he droned.”

Moran went on: “I think as a replacement, he’s just cursing...and that’ll get a charge, you know, to say the F word or whatever.”

A spokesperson for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Throughout Trump’s second term, reports have detailed his profane tirades against his own appointees behind closed doors. In public, too, the president has repeatedly unleashed expletive-laden posts on Truth Social.

“The only thing [Iran has] is FAKE NEWS from the USA, a willingness to kill their protesters (now over 100,000 people dead. They must be tried for war crimes against humanity!), and a good line of “bulls--t,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. “Thank you for your attention to this matter!”

Trump’s crude language has also featured prominently on the campaign trail ahead of the midterm elections. As he has traversed the country in recent weeks in a last-ditch effort to drum up support for his endorsed candidates, some—including the candidates themselves—have argued that his appearances are doing more harm than good.

The president’s campaign blitz comes amid low approval ratings, voter frustration over the cost of living and high gas prices, and his deeply unpopular war on Iran. His speeches have frequently veered into headline-grabbing outbursts.

At a rally in Nebraska earlier this month, for example, Trump appeared to suggest that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego as a “small price to pay” for keeping the country and the world safe. He later clarified his remarks at a rally in Texas.

Whether Trump helps sink his party in November or not, Moran argued that the cultural shift toward profanity he has fostered will endure.

“He gives permission to people to liberate themselves from the strictures of decency, to become the worst version of themselves. And I think, I mean, I don’t think we’re gonna come back from it for a while,” Moran said.

“I think we are a different country. And I think that potty mouth is his liberation and his temptation,” he continued. “Because the thing about Trumpism, and this is why it’s going to be difficult, once you’ve bought in—it’s hard to get out. Once you’ve accepted this is the standard of our politics, of your own standard as a citizen.”

news.title: Trump Defends Russia Sanctions Waiver Amid Republican Backlash
news.text: President Donald Trump is defending his decision to waive key sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia, after Republicans accused him of undermining support for Ukraine and "capitulating" to Russian President Vladimir Putin. In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump said enforcing the measures risked derailing negotiations to end the conflict in Ukraine, insisting that progress was being made in diplomatic discussions. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one,” Trump wrote. “I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” Trump said he could sign the document later but that he wanted to avoid antagonizing Russia because he believes Moscow might otherwise increase its support for Iran. “Perhaps more importantly, Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing,” Trump wrote. He also accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of hurting U.S. interests by targeting Russian diesel refineries, adding that “farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this." Meanwhile, Trump wrote, Russia was continuing to send millions of barrels of diesel to world markets at low prices. Trump even claimed the Zelensky "doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did." Zelensky has not publicly responded to Trump's latest comment but he had previously criticized Trump's decision to lift the sanctions. The president also faced significant backlash from members of his own party, including Sen. Thom Tillis, who called the move “beyond irresponsible,” and Rep. Don Bacon, who warned that Trump was “prolonging the war, not ending it." Newsweek has reached out to the White House for comment. Trump's Sanctions Waiver: What To Know The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 was designed to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its war against Ukraine, including through tariffs targeting countries that continue purchasing Russian energy. Trump signed the legislation on September 18. But in an executive order issued Friday, he waived the application of key sanctions, restrictions and tariffs, citing U.S. national interests. The additional penalties were scheduled to begin Sunday but will remain on hold while the waiver is in force. The administration has indicated that the decision may not be final. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Trump wants up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of imposing the sanctions and tariffs, after the president signed an order waiving the measures on Friday. Republicans Criticize Decision To Lift Sanctions Several Republicans have argued that Trump's decision runs counter to the purpose of the sanctions law and risks weakening Washington's ability to pressure Putin. Rep. Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, warned that, "the President is prolonging the war, not ending it," while Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, referring to the late Senator Lindsey Graham, whose name is attached to the legislation, wrote: “Lindsey would be appalled.” Senator Ted Cruz called the waiver a mistake, adding that the administration should have considered other ways to lower fuel prices. “The current path, unfortunately, just benefits Putin," he warned. Sen. Tillis agreed, writing on X, “It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day." Tillis also questioned why the administration would not enforce legislation that passed the Senate 86-11, and argued Trump should address the war with Iran to lower energy prices rather than “doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.” Rep. French Hill of Arkansas said the United States should be increasing economic pressure on Russia rather than easing it. He also said he had requested a classified briefing on the administration's reasoning. The criticism has not been limited to Republicans. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Richard Blumenthal, both Democrats, have also condemned the waiver, arguing that it benefits Moscow while Russia's invasion continues. Not every lawmaker opposed the sanctions waiver. Republican Senator James Lankford, of Oklahoma, said the president was attempting to balance pressure on Russia with the need to address high energy prices affecting American households, during a Sunday appearance on NBC's Meet the Press. “The president has the ability under the statute to be able to look at national interests,” Lankford said. “He's trying to walk this fine balance." Lankford argued that the waiver did not mean Trump was siding with Putin, pointing to continued U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, the provision of weapons and other sanctions imposed on Russian oil companies. “Any belief that President Trump is aligning with President Putin is not true,” Lankford said. However, Lankford acknowledged the underlying dispute over Russian energy purchases. He said the United States should not buy Russian oil directly, while arguing that domestic energy production and refinery capacity were important to reducing prices. The White House has defended Trump's decision, saying that enforcing the sanctions immediately would impede U.S. efforts to negotiate a comprehensive peace agreement. “The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests,” White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement Saturday. Energy Prices and the Russian Diesel Deal The sanctions controversy follows Trump's announcement of an agreement with Putin to increase Russian diesel supplies to global markets, a move the president said could help ease energy costs. The agreement has also drawn bipartisan opposition. A group of 12 senators urged Trump in an October 13 letter to rescind the deal, warning that increased Russian energy sales could provide Moscow with additional revenue to fund its war against Ukraine. The senators argued that allowing Russia to sell diesel more freely would undermine U.S. security interests and weaken support for Ukraine. The sanctions waiver and diesel agreement are related to the administration's broader effort to address energy prices, but the executive order does not specifically mention the diesel deal. Rubio has defended the administration's approach, saying the review period would allow officials to assess the economic effects of enforcing the sanctions. The administration has argued that energy-market stability and diplomatic negotiations must be considered alongside the objective of pressuring Russia. Critics counter that easing restrictions could undermine the sanctions' intended purpose at a time when Russian attacks on Ukraine continue. Ukraine Pushes Back Zelensky has criticized Trump's decision to waive the sanctions, warning that easing pressure on Moscow could encourage further Russian aggression rather than help bring the war to an end. “The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” Zelensky wrote on X on Saturday. “It definitely helps only the Russians,” he added. Zelensky also warned that the sanctions waiver could signal the beginning of further concessions to Moscow, pointing to Trump's separate agreement to increase Russian diesel supplies to global markets. “I believe the Diesel Deal is the first step. Unfortunately, I don't think Putin can be stopped this way,” Zelensky told reporters. “On the contrary, he feels pleased and happy to have this kind of support.” His comments came after Russian forces launched attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, striking more than 15 power generation and transmission sites, according to Zelensky. The attacks have heightened concerns over Ukraine's ability to maintain electricity and heating supplies as winter approaches. Zelensky urged Trump to use his position to press Putin to halt the attacks and end the war, while maintaining that weakening sanctions would not achieve that goal.
news.summary: President Donald Trump is defending his decision to waive key sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia.
