news.title: Egypt says ready to back Saudi Arabia in war against Iran-allied Houthis
news.text:
CAIRO — Regional military power Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, potentially raising the stakes in the Middle East war as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on the kingdom.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested an urgent parliament session to authorize the military, one of the Arab world’s largest, to help defend its Gulf Arab ally if the kingdom requested its support.

A parliamentary vote had been expected on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said.

Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognized government and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the north, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Any Egyptian military backing for Saudi Arabia could mark a major escalation in the wider Iran war, which has threatened global energy supplies and sent oil prices soaring since the US and Israel attacked the Islamic Republic in late February.

Hours after an announcement on further discussions by the parliament, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said in a post on X that he discussed regional developments and the importance of de-escalation during a phone call with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan.

HOUTHIS RAMP UP ATTACKS ON SAUDI ARABIA
The Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh’s international airport and the ​state oil company Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with Saudi-backed forces. The Houthi advances threaten the strategic Bab el-Mandeb oil shipping route, following the collapse of a truce.

“Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites,” the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.

The statement followed a meeting of Egypt’s National Defense Council chaired by Mr. Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.

Mr. Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Mr. Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.

If Egypt weighs in, it could face attacks by the Houthis, ragtag mountain fighters who have emerged as a deadly force of tens of thousands and whose missiles and drones threaten the region.

Arab countries, especially Gulf states hosting US bases, have faced repeated attacks by Iran and its allies, including the Houthis and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq, during the conflict.

Egypt’s Mediterranean port of Damietta came under a drone attack in July with no group claiming responsibility. Egypt has not blamed any party for the attack but said it was taking necessary measures to protect the country’s national security.

Egypt and ​Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi ​Arabia and ⁠other oil-rich Gulf states including the United Arab Emirates provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist President Mohamed ⁠Morsi ​in 2013. Mr. Sisi became president a year later.

Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role in the civil war.

Riyadh has turned to regional allies and Pakistan after it sought US President Donald Trump’s help to fight the Houthis. Mr. Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing.

Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman visited Abu Dhabi on Sunday and met with UAE President Mohammed bin ​Zayed Al Nahyan, with talks focusing on regional security, according to the Emirati state news agency.

The talks followed a visit to Riyadh last month by UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the first trip by ‌a senior UAE official to the kingdom since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year. — Reuters

news.title: Macron expresses 'anger and shame' after 2,400 arrested in violent France protests
news.text: French President Emmanuel Macron has voiced the nation's "anger" and "shame" over sweeping protests against soaring living costs and deteriorating school conditions, which have led to at least 2,400 arrests. Mr Macron echoed fellow government officials in attributing much of the violence to far-left activists, accusing them of targeting police and public buildings in a bid to stoke disorder. "Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," Mr Macron declared in a televised address to the country. He condemned "unrestrained violence" by "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals". Mr Macron had earlier convened an emergency meeting with senior government figures, a day after masked groups set buildings ablaze and stormed public properties, including town halls, across several cities. He revealed he had directed prefects to collaborate with mayors to safeguard public buildings and businesses over the coming weeks, including imposing protest bans where necessary. In the central town of Limoges, fire tore through the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to cave in and leaving the building on the verge of total destruction. Hundreds of demonstrators once again gathered on Sunday at the Place de la Republique in Paris , amid a significant police presence. Officers deployed tear gas as sporadic tensions flared across the area, with small clusters of individuals attempting to set bicycles and bins alight. "The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not," interior minister Laurent Nunez wrote on X, pointing to the ransacking of hundreds of businesses across cities including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux. Official figures put Saturday's march attendance at approximately 550,000, while organisers claimed the figure was closer to 800,000. Protesters heeded calls from a trade union, student groups and activists seeking to reignite the "yellow vest" movement, which first emerged in 2018 as a demonstration against social inequality. Large-scale demonstrations in France are frequently tarnished by violence on the periphery of otherwise peaceful marches, resulting in confrontations with police. The number of arrests reported on Sunday came close to the nearly 2,000 recorded across the country during a single day of yellow-vest protests back in December 2018. One individual suffered a fatal heart attack, according to a statement from Paris police, though no further details were provided. The Paris prosecutors' office confirmed it had launched an investigation. Around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday morning, the aftermath of the unrest was plain to see, with uprooted cobblestones, smashed shopfronts and shards of broken glass littering the streets. Reports of looting and damage emerged from around the square and several other tourist and shopping districts in the city centre. Paris police confirmed 855 arrests in the capital region, with the city's prosecutor's office stating that 557 people remained in custody. "I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed," said Marie Peyreigne, a 57 year old government employee, as she tried to make sense of the chaos that had unfolded. Surveying the wreckage, scores of Parisians photographed the partially demolished base of the central monument at Place de la Republique - a statue of Marianne, an enduring symbol of France. Jean Foissy, 74, said he had intended to join the demonstration but encountered "a wall of riot police and fires everywhere", and turned back. "I was very scared," he said. "I've been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me." Margaux Eude, 26, said she backs the protest movement but "didn't think it would escalate like this". "It's the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimises the movement", she said. Political figures across the divide moved swiftly to exploit the fallout from Saturday's unrest for political gain, with one eye firmly on next spring's presidential election. Far-right leader and presidential contender Marine Le Pen rounded on far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon, who had taken part in the Paris march. "Looting, ransacking, destroying and attacking law enforcement: Rioters have again spoiled the October 17 demonstrations for the protection of purchasing power," Ms Le Pen wrote on X. Her running mate, Jordan Bardella, said on X that "if the silent majority of French decide it, we will re-establish order for the long-term". Mr Melenchon, for his part, exchanged sharp words with the prime minister, accusing Mr Lecornu of "playing with fire" and claiming that "by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers' unions". Mr Melenchon stated that "my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction". US President Donald Trump posted "France is burning!" on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to "the immigration of people from an entirely different world ". "Close your borders and take control, before it is too late!" he wrote. French authorities and police have drawn no connection between immigrants and the rioting, repeatedly attributing elements of the violence to "radical far-left groups" and opportunistic looters. Paris mayor Emmanuel Gregoire announced the establishment of an emergency unit to help businesses evaluate the extent of the damage. "The scale of the damage is considerable and unprecedented," Mr Gregoire wrote in an open letter. "Paris is a city of freedoms, debate and demonstrations. It must remain so. But it must also be a city where everyone can work and run a business safely." The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, France's three biggest cities, called for an urgent meeting with the prime minister in the coming days "given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation." In the southern coastal city of Marseille, demonstrators temporarily stormed the entrance hall of City Hall, while a group wearing hoods and masks vandalised a police station. In Lyon, flames erupted within a tourist office. In Limoges, a band of "radical troublemakers" broke into City Hall while elected officials, staff, security personnel and members of the public were inside, Maurice Barate, prefect of the Haute-Vienne region, said. "Despite the presence of so many people, they deliberately set the building on fire. It is an extremely serious and unspeakable act," he said. In eastern France, the Mulhouse prosecutor's office said an investigation has been launched after a 17 year old girl sustained injuries during the protests and lost an eye. On Saturday, another investigation was launched after a young demonstrator lost a hand in Saint-Etienne. The injuries emerge as police face intense criticism over their deployment of grenades and other riot-control weapons during recent demonstrations.
news.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron has spoken of "anger" and "shame" as nationwide protests in France over the cost of living crisis and school conditions turned violent, resulting in at least 2,400 arrests across Paris and other cities.

news.title: Nothing left to loot: Parisians ponder the real cost of another night of riots
news.text:
Every action is dominated by men in their late teens and early 20s, almost all wearing their black uniforms. Young women can also be seen in the crowd, but they are in the minority among those provoking the police.

When the masks are lowered, the faces reflect modern France: the skin tones are white, black and brown. But the white faces are relatively rare. The crowd is overwhelmingly made up of young men who are new to France or born to migrant families, although there is no time to stop and ask whether their French citizenship goes back one, two, three or more generations.

This is a delicate subject because of the argument about whether the riots in France are caused by migration. Donald Trump insists they are; his critics say they are not. The debate about causation is surely complex. But it is important to be honest about the reality on the streets, rather than waving away what is obvious to every passer-by in Paris.

The streets around the Place de la Republique are full of young men from migrant backgrounds who seemed primed for confrontations with authority. They try to test the police, then retreat and scatter into small groups. In one moment they are protesters, in the next they look like bystanders.

The confrontations continue into the night, and there is some opportunistic looting. Two men clamber out of a homewares store carrying brand new wheelie-bags; two boys then try to climb over the broken sheet glass to see if they can find something for themselves.
news.summary: They began as a protest against conditions in schools, burgeoned into a wider movement against the cost of living, and at the weekend, became an orgy of destruction. Reporting from Paris, David Crowe finds a modern France facing up to troubled times.

news.title: Trump defends Russia sanctions waiver
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 19 (IANS) US President Donald Trump defended his decision to suspend sweeping new sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia and major buyers of Russian energy, saying he did not want to undermine negotiations aimed at ending the war in Ukraine. The President's latest explanation came two days after he signed an executive order waiving major provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, including additional tariffs that could have affected India because of its purchases of Russian oil. Trump said his administration was making progress towards a negotiated settlement and suggested that imposing fresh economic penalties at this stage could push Moscow away from the negotiating table. "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social. The President also linked his decision to developments involving Iran and global energy markets. He argued that Russia was providing less assistance to Iran than it potentially could and said he wanted to preserve that situation. He also criticised Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel refineries, arguing that disruptions to fuel supplies were affecting consumers and businesses internationally. Under the executive order signed on Friday, the administration formally provided for tariffs of 500 per cent on certain Russian goods and 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, subject to statutory conditions. However, the same order waived the application of those additional duties and most of the new sanctions provisions. The waiver does not remove existing US sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders against Russia. For India, the decision is significant because the legislation could expose major purchasers of Russian energy to additional US tariffs. The waiver means those new duties are not being applied under the order at present. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the administration needed time to assess the wider economic consequences of imposing the sanctions and tariffs. Rubio specifically identified India among the countries that could be affected by the legislation. He indicated that Trump wanted to use a period of up to 60 days to consider the implications for the global economy and the United States before determining the next course of action. It provides that the waivers will remain effective until the President or the Secretary of State, following the required consultations, determines that further action is appropriate. The decision has drawn criticism from lawmakers who favour stronger economic pressure on Moscow. Several Republicans and Democrats have questioned whether suspending the sanctions would weaken Washington's leverage over Russia at a time when the conflict in Ukraine continues. The White House has defended the waiver as consistent with efforts to secure a negotiated peace agreement. Trump's latest remarks also underscored his differences with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over the conduct of the war and its economic consequences. The Graham Act, signed into law on September 18, was designed to strengthen economic pressure on Russia through sanctions, restrictions and tariffs, including measures affecting countries purchasing Russian energy. It also gave the President authority to waive specified provisions after certifying to Congress that doing so served US national interests.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine’s use of the SpaceX satellite network remains partially restricted, Axios reported.

“Secretary Rubio said no one at the White House ordered it to be slowed down this week so that drones couldn’t use it. But effectively, that was the outcome,” Brennan said before playing Rubio’s remarks.

Rubio said “nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened. But my understanding is it’s been restored.” He made the remarks Saturday evening before leaving on a trip to India, according to Axios.

“Absolutely not. I mean, this is something where there needs to be an investigation. There needs to be a congressional investigation,” Turner said.

The congressman added that weapons meant for Ukraine, funding and intelligence have broken down before, only for it to come out later that “unnamed people in the Pentagon perhaps break it.”

“We need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things,” he said.

Ukrainian officials say the network, which once worked on drones flying 400 kilometers per hour, now cuts off at 161 kilometers per hour, Axios reported. A White House official told the outlet, “we didn’t slow down Starlink at all, and the service is currently operational.”

Later on in the interview with Brennan, Turner said that President Donald Trump has the authority to impose the sanctions he waived under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 and that “I would encourage him to do so.” He also said the European Union is the “fourth largest offender” in buying energy from Russia.

Turner faces Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, a nurse practitioner and Air Force veteran, in the November election, according to the Dayton Daily News. The nonpartisan Cook Political report rates the race as “Lean R.”

Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving the Russian sanctions and tariffs required under the law, which he signed on Sept. 18.
news.summary: ‘There needs to be a congressional investigation.’

news.title: Ukraine launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia as spat between Trump and Zelensky continues
news.text:
Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war.

The strikes came as tensions between Kyiv and Washington deepened, with US President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure and the prospect of further US sanctions against Moscow still uncertain.

Trump said Sunday that he decided to hold off on implementing new sanctions on Russia because he doesn’t “want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”

In a social media post, the US president defended his Friday order to issue a waiver to prevent new sanctions from being placed on Moscow from bipartisan criticism that he was favoring Russian President Vladimir Putin’s interests over those of Ukraine. Trump said he believed new sanctions would undermine negotiations to bring about a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine.

“I can sign it later, or any time that I want!” Trump added of the sanctions.

Trump also lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who has been critical of Trump’s recent outreach to Putin, for launching strikes on Russian energy infrastructure during the conflict, claiming Zelensky “doesn’t want to end this war.”

Zelensky: Waiving sanctions strengthens Russia

Speaking on NBC’s “Meet the Press” earlier on Sunday, Zelensky said waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen Putin’s war effort. He also said US-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being “blocked for some period of time.”

Zelensky said that while he trusted Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a “historic mistake” for Washington.

“People want to forget what’s going on. But we can’t give this possibility to forget, or to change reality, or to change the truth,” Zelensky said. “We can’t compare me and Putin. He’s (an) aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He’s a terrorist. And that’s why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position.”

Later Sunday, Zelensky said on social media that he had spoken with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an Oct. 9 meeting between US and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami, as well as “next steps in diplomacy.”

Two killed as Russia and Ukraine trade blows

One person was killed and five others were wounded in the St. Petersburg attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, local Gov. Alexander Beglov said. A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center operated by Russian tech giant VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed.

Russia’s Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Kyiv was “resisting” Moscow’s invasion but could not “change the current course of events.”

Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a woman was killed and a 6-year-old girl was among at least two other people wounded in two Russian attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Sunday.

Russia continues energy attacks, Kyiv says

Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4½-year-old war, but offered no details. Kyiv reported Russian attacks on energy sites continued after Trump’s announcement, and on Thursday said it had resumed strikes on Russian oil facilities after a three-day pause.

Zelensky wrote on X on Sunday that Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times in the week since Trump’s announcement. The Ukrainian government initially said it was observing the ceasefire.

Energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions were struck overnight, leaving tens of thousands of families without power, he said, accusing Russia of trying to cause a blackout.

“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting,” the Ukrainian president wrote.

Ukraine apology to Lithuania over drone alert

Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry apologized on Sunday after a drone entered Lithuania’s airspace, prompting authorities to issue an air raid warning.

Russian electronic warfare may have diverted the drone during a Ukrainian operation against legitimate military targets in Russia, ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement.

Lithuanian authorities urged residents in two northern counties along the Latvian border to take cover early Sunday because of a possible drone incursion, public broadcaster LRT reported.

A drone entered the northern Pasvalys region and damaged a moving car, LRT said, citing Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Center. No injuries were reported.

news.title: Ukraine's Fate Without Ukraine? Putin Floats Trump-Xi Summit to End War
news.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss the war in Ukraine, in a move that could raise concerns among Kyiv and its European allies, according to The Wall Street Journal. The proposed summit would aim to negotiate an end to the four-year conflict on terms favourable to Moscow, the newspaper reported, citing people familiar with the discussions. Such a meeting, if held without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, would be unprecedented and could trigger alarm in European capitals, the report said. Putin reportedly raised the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump on 9 October. The call also resulted in an agreement for the US to buy Russian diesel fuel and help facilitate its sale on the global market, according to the report. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions about a possible meeting were under way, but said no firm arrangements had been made. "There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place," he told The Wall Street Journal. A senior US official said Trump had not agreed to the summit, although he could be receptive to the proposal as he seeks to fulfil his campaign pledge to end the war. Trump had promised to end the conflict on "day one" of his new term, but is now approaching nearly two years in office. Putin Seeks Summit on Chinese Soil The Kremlin has suggested holding the proposed talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for 18 and 19 November in Shenzhen, a major technology hub in southern China, according to people familiar with the discussions. Russian officials have raised the proposal with Beijing through diplomatic channels. People close to recent discussions between Moscow and Beijing told the newspaper that China had indicated it would not object to the meeting if Trump agreed. A trilateral summit in China could strengthen Xi's position as an international mediator and enhance Beijing's role in diplomacy between major powers, analysts said. "China wants to be seen as the pivot of the great powers, and potentially as a mediator between the U.S. and Russia," said Yun Sun, director of the China programme at the Stimson Center, a Washington-based think tank. Putin has proposed trilateral meetings with Trump and Xi on previous occasions, according to a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. The latest proposal comes as Moscow's relations with Washington have shown signs of warming. Trump Faces Pressure Over Russia Policy Trump has recently reached an agreement involving Russian diesel supplies in an effort to bring down fuel prices, which have weighed on the US economy and could affect Republican prospects in the midterm elections. On Friday, Trump halted the implementation of sanctions against Russia that were due to be imposed under a bipartisan bill he signed last month. The move drew criticism from lawmakers, including some of his allies. A senior White House official said Trump had made the decisions after concluding that there were few other good options for reducing prices. Energy experts, however, broadly agree that the war with Iran is the main cause of rising diesel prices. They also believe the volume of fuel Russia has promised to supply would have only a limited effect on the market. Trump's approach to the war in Ukraine has also included renewed criticism of Zelenskyy. The US president has urged his Ukrainian counterpart to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries and suggested that Ukraine needs a new president. Meanwhile, US-led efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict have largely stalled. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy following a Ukrainian strike on an oil terminal in St Petersburg, Putin's hometown, earlier that day. Trump accused the Ukrainian leader of targeting Russian diesel refineries and said Zelenskyy "doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did". The US president also defended his decision to hold off on imposing sanctions, saying he did not want to push Russia away from negotiations. "I WANT THIS WAR END!" Trump wrote.
news.summary: If held, this unprecedented summit could occur during the APEC summit in China next month

news.title: Trump Says Russia Sanctions Waiver Is to Keep Moscow at Negotiating Table
news.text:
WASHINGTON—President Donald Trump on Oct. 18 defended his decision to waive Russia sanctions, arguing that it’s essential to keeping Moscow at the negotiating table in talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.

“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he wrote in a Truth Social post.

“Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations! Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!”

Legislation championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and signed into law by Trump on Sept. 18 would have imposed sanctions on the top five countries that purchase oil and gas from Russia over its war against Ukraine.

In an interview with Meet the Press, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called Trump’s decision to waive Russia sanctions a “historic mistake” and “big support” for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The sanctions waiver came days after Trump reached a deal with Moscow to supply diesel to the global market, including the United States, to lower fuel prices.

Another 3 million tons of diesel could be delivered depending on the condition of Russia’s refineries, Trump added.

Trump defended the sanctions waiver after growing criticism that he is helping Moscow continue its war against Ukraine.

He added in his Oct. 18 post that Moscow “is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

“I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way,” he added.

He continued his criticism of Zelenskyy, echoing remarks he had made in recent days.

“Zelenskyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States,” he wrote. “Farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this.”

Trump also said that the Ukrainian leader appeared indifferent to his warnings, accusing him of not wanting to end the war.

He also reiterated that Zelenskyy missed an opportunity to negotiate a more favorable agreement to end the war two years ago.

“His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead,” Trump wrote.
news.summary: The president said he doesn’t want to do anything that would ‘drive, foolishly, Russia away.’

news.title: Condition make crayfish bend
news.text:
Many of the [on the one hand] spectacular and [on the other hand] curious events and statements that dominated the national political scene last week recall the old saying of hard-pressed city proletarians, that “na condition make crayfish bend.”

Beginning with the late start of this year’s election campaign. With about 90 days to the start of 2027 general and presidential elections, it was a curiosity that campaigns by political parties, both ruling and opposition, were hardly in full swing. By this time in previous elections, every inch on walls and buildings were splashed with posters; huge campaign billboards welcomed you into every town; vehicles blaring with campaign music were positioned in all markets and street corners; radio and TV stations engaged in endless political programs while campaign rallies, the most conspicuous element of Nigerian campaigns, were holding in every town, with motorists and motorcyclists charging through city streets and often knocking down by-standers.

Probably the most hectic national campaign we ever had was in 1978-79, which lasted from November 1978, when the five registered parties nominated their candidates, until July-August 1979, when five rounds of elections were held. The late Dr. Rufai Ibrahim wrote in Daily Times that he went on a national political reporting tour and ran into GNPP candidate Waziri Ibrahim nearly 20 times. NPN candidate Alhaji Shehu Shagari visited not only state capitals but every major town in every one of the then 19 states and, according to Ibrahim, he was always lodged in the best house in a town, belonging to an NPN chieftain. UPN’s Chief Awolowo also made a big splash by hopping around the country in a helicopter, which always attracted great curiosity. This year, campaigns are starting quite late.

Better late than never, is another common Nigerian saying. On Wednesday last week, October 15, the ruling APC inaugurated its Presidential Campaign Council [PCC] at a major ceremony in Abuja. Major, because the entire Federal cabinet, National Assembly leaders and most of its members, 33 serving state governors [out of 36] and numerous former governors and ministers, as well as the Vice President and the President, were all present.

Yet, the biggest curiosity to come out of the occasion was the revelation, earlier speculated by a newspaper, then confirmed by the campaign’s director general and finally endorsed by the President, was that President Bola Tinubu will not visit all the states during this campaign. Indeed, the schedule of rallies later released by the campaign team said he will personally campaign in 12 states [one third of the total] beginning in Kaduna on October 25 and rounding up in Lagos on January 9.

The large number of today’s states must be a factor. In the Second Republic, Shagari had only 19 states to visit. In the Third Republic, MKO Abiola and Bashir Tofa had 30 states to visit, but since 1999, Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Yar’adua, Goodluck Jonathan, Muhammadu Buhari and Tinubu too in 2023 have had to personally campaign in 36 states. A presidential campaign rally in a state is politically important because it energises party supporters, attracts the greatest media attention and elicits the greatest youth excitement. But beyond the podium speeches, it also enables private meetings with party leaders and personal promises. On the flip side, it affords candidates more opportunity for gaffes.

The President said at the event that he will refrain from touring the whole country so that he will concentrate on governance issues. I can imagine the sweat on the brows of top presidential aides and communicators as they worked out how to present this bombshell announcement. In a liberal democracy, governance and campaigning are not mutually exclusive. This spin further raised eyebrows at a time when television pictures show US President Donald Trump vigorously campaigning across his country for the midterm elections, even though he himself is not on the ballot. President Tinubu said he will leave governors and other APC leaders to take the campaign to the LGAs and wards. One mischievous young lad asked if it means governors will abandon governance while they campaign.

A curious presence at the APC council inauguration were three men: Governors Charles Soludo of Anambra and Ademola Adeleke of Osun, and FCT Minister Nyesom Wike, an alleged member of the opposition PDP. Adeleke entertained the event with his sartorial dance steps. The three men were later additions to the campaign council, a first in Nigerian politics, when prominent members of opposition parties openly campaigned for the ruling party’s candidate. Adeleke’s Accord Party even has a presidential candidate, Gbenga Olawepo-Hashim, even though the party disowned him. This was reminiscent of 2003, when Alliance for Democracy [AD] refused to field a presidential candidate and instead supported PDP’s candidate, President Obasanjo. Curiously, then Lagos State Governor Bola Tinubu was the only AD governor who disagreed with his colleagues’ dangerous gambit. Accord and APGA may be towing AD’s path to ruination today.

Only three serving governors remained outside the APC umbrella. One of them is Oyo State governor Seyi Makinde, who is APM’s presidential candidate. Another is Bauchi’s Bala Mohammed, who is an APM senatorial candidate. Third one is Abia State governor Alex Otti, who remarkably remained in LP despite the defection of its former presidential candidate and top rallying point Peter Obi, now NDC’s presidential candidate. Otti apparently believes he can win reelection on the strength of his own record and on the apparent unpopularity of APC in the Southeast region.

Three days after the APC council launch, there was another grand ceremony in Abuja to launch Arewa for Asiwaju, A4A. It was an impressive array of Administration officials and lots of former governors and ministers of Northern extraction. Although it was not expressly stated, the launch of this group, led by former Kano State governor Ibrahim Shekarau, is a response to the slipping popularity of the Administration in the North, mostly occasioned by insecurity, the difficult socio-economic conditions, as well as perceptions of regionally lopsided projects and appointments.

Vice President Kashim Shettima’s statement at the launch, that “the North has nothing to fear” from a Tinubu second term was, without saying so, an apparent response to what other regional groups were saying, that “if he did this to us in his first term, what will he do to us in his second term?” While APC national chairman Nentawe Yilwatda said the North will award the APC ticket 70% of its votes [how did he arrive at that figure?], Shettima rather carefully said the North will support the ticket but that the support is not unconditional, but will be earned through “facts, radical transparency, measurable results and honest engagement with citizens about ongoing reforms.”

The ruling party having opened the way, major opposition parties ADC and NDC are set to launch their own campaign councils and kick off their rallies soon. Even as they gear up for that, there was still talk in the air of their presenting a single candidate to confront the APC behemoth. A committee led by former APC Northwest zonal chairman Salihu Lukman has been working on this through the G100 group. It is however difficult to see if this could be still be done given the short time remaining. There is also the problem of the apparent non-transferability of the major candidate’s political bases. In the 2023 elections, Peter Obi generated his most support in the Southeast, Lagos, Plateau and Nasarawa; Atiku Abubakar swept the Northeast and majority of Northwest states as well as Osun, while then NNPP candidate Rabiu Kwankwaso swept Kano. Given the regional slant of their support bases, it is not at all clear that if one of the major opposition candidates were to step down, he could transfer his base of support to the other.

Right now, NDC presidential running mate Kwankwaso has a big problem on his hands in the disqualification of Kano NDC’s governorship candidate Aminu Abdussalam Gwarzo. His name was excluded from INEC’s final list of candidates, alongside others, on the grounds that his name was not on the membership register that NDC submitted to INEC in May, as per the recent Supreme Court ruling. If this stance stands, Kwankwaso’s bid to dislodge his former protégé Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf has developed a big K-leg. The old warhorse that he is however, he might yet throw his weight behind one of the small parties’ candidates.

APM’s presidential candidate Seyi Makinde caused further bending of the crayfish by nominating former DSS director general Lawal Daura as his running mate. Daura has been lying low since 2017, when then Acting President Yemi Osinbajo sacked him because he sent DSS agents to storm the National Assembly. President Buhari did not restore him when he returned from his sick leave, but Daura is now hankering after Osinbajo’s old seat.

Late last week, Senate President Godswill Akpabio bent the crayfish until its back almost snapped when he got the Senate to adopt a resolution saying the Senate to be inaugurated in June next year, after the elections, must retain him and other leaders of the current Assembly in their seats. Constitutional, administrative, legal, procedural, parliamentary, political and ethical eyebrows were all raised following the announcement. 

Not to be outdone, Works Minister Dave Umahi announced last week that President Tinubu had done a “wondering engineering decision” by approving the bending of the Lags-Calabar coastal highway road project to enter the existing East-West road. In other words, the coastal road bent like a crayfish until its carapace, chelipod, telson and antennae snapped, eliciting loud protests from Bayelsa State government officials. They said their state’s marshy terrain is not unconquerable by road engineers because Governor Duoye Diri built one road with up to 20 bridges on it. Talk about condition making crayfish to bend.

news.title: "We asked European allies to put secondary tariffs on India and China for buying Russian oil, they refused: Scott Bessent
news.text:
Washington DC [US], October 18 (ANI): US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said European countries refused Washington's request to impose secondary tariffs on India and China for purchasing Russian oil, questioning why the United States should bear the economic burden of pressuring Moscow alone.

Bessent, in an interview with NBC, said the Trump administration had approached its European allies in the spring to seek coordinated action against countries importing Russian energy.

"So we have asked-in the spring, I asked our European allies to join us in putting secondary tariffs on China, on India. They refused. So why should the US bear the burden?" Bessent said.

He added that US President Donald Trump wanted the fighting in Ukraine to stop and that the proposed sanctions legislation provided the administration with time to assess the situation.

"President Trump has made it clear he wants the killing to stop. And the so-called Graham bill gives the president the flexibility, gives him 60 days to assess the situation," he said.

Bessent also criticised European countries for continuing to purchase Russian energy, citing shipments from Russia's Yamal facility.

"In the first 6 months of the year, there were 140 cargoes that left. 136 of those went to Europe-to Belgium, to Spain, to France, to the Netherlands-over USD 8 billion," he said, arguing that European countries had provided Russia with substantial revenue while supporting Ukraine.

His remarks come after Trump temporarily waived certain sanctions and tariff provisions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, allowing the administration 60 days to assess the potential economic consequences of implementing the measures.

The legislation would have allowed tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported into the United States from the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas, including India and China.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday described India as an important ally, saying Washington needed to consider its energy requirements before imposing tariffs or sanctions.

"These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries-India, for example, and others," Rubio said, adding that the administration wanted to evaluate the implications for the global and US economies.

Rubio also noted that countries such as India had diversified their energy supplies but could not immediately stop importing Russian energy.

The US administration's decision comes amid continuing pressure on global energy supplies due to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and escalating tensions in the Middle East.

Bessent said Washington could engage with European partners again, questioning why the United States should act alone in imposing economic pressure on Moscow. (ANI)
